Stream Annotation Protocol

A short guide to how we annotate image streams and what the resulting labels mean.

Contents
  1. Overview
  2. Inputs
  3. The annotation GUI
  4. How to annotate
  5. Spatial‑temporal location: (frame_idx, traversal_idx)
  6. Example data & launching the server
  7. Output format
  8. Possible extensions

1. Overview

We start with a sequence of images (a video-like stream from a moving camera) and a predefined set of interesting objects (labels). For each frame in which an object of interest is visible, the annotator clicks a single point on the object and assigns it a label.

The camera may revisit the same scene multiple times. Each revisit is called a traversal. Whenever the stream starts a new pass through the scene, the annotator presses the New traverse? button so that frame is tagged as the start of a new traversal. This lets us recover the spatial‑temporal location of each object — in particular, the latest traversal in which it appears.

2. Inputs

  • Image folder. A flat directory of frames in stream order, e.g. example_data/stream/28_metfloor_first150/images/. Filenames typically encode timestamps so lexicographic order matches temporal order.
  • Label JSON. A predefined list of categories of interest, e.g. label_28_metfloor.json. Either a bare list or {"labels": [...]} is accepted.

3. The annotation GUI

  • Image list (left). Green dots = frames with labeled points; grey dots = frames marked complete with no objects; missing dot = unannotated.
  • Canvas (center). Click a point on the object, then click a label below to assign the category. Multiple labeled points per frame are allowed.
  • Label palette (bottom). The fixed set of objects of interest for this stream.
  • New traverse? (top-right). Toggle to mark the current frame as the start of a new traversal. The Traversal counter to its right shows the index of the current traversal.
  • Navigation. ← / → moves between frames and auto-saves. An empty annotation list still counts as "completed" (the frame contains no objects of interest).

4. How to annotate

  1. Walk through the stream in order with ← / →.
  2. If the current frame shows an object from the label set, click the object, then click its label. Repeat for additional objects.
  3. If the frame has no objects of interest, just advance — the empty list is recorded.
  4. When you see that the camera has begun a new pass through the scene (revisiting earlier ground), press New traverse? on that first frame of the new pass. Leave it off for all other frames.
Press New traverse? once, on the first frame of each new pass. The traversal index for subsequent frames is derived automatically by counting how many new_traversal: true flags have been seen so far.

5. Spatial‑temporal location: (frame_idx, traversal_idx)

Every annotated point is implicitly tagged with two indices:

  • frame_idx — position of the frame in the stream (0-based).
  • traversal_idx — which pass through the scene this frame belongs to.

Downstream tasks consume the latest occurrence of each object on the time axis: the highest traversal_idx in which the object is annotated, and the frame within that traversal where it appears. This is how we capture "where the object ended up" after the scene was re-arranged across passes.

Traversal 1 Traversal 2 (starts at new_traversal: true) Traversal 3 (starts at new_traversal: true) ⚑ = annotator pressed New traverse?

In the illustration, the tomato was annotated in all three traversals; its latest location is (frame_idx = 15, traversal_idx = 2). The pepper was missing from traversal 2 but reappeared in traversal 3 at (frame_idx = 13, traversal_idx = 2). Downstream code picks these last-appearance entries as each object's authoritative position.

ObjectTraversals seenLatest (frame_idx, traversal_idx)
🍅 tomato1 2 3(15, 2)
🥔 pepper1 3(13, 2)
Indexing note. traversal_idx is 0-based: the first traversal is index 0, and each new_traversal: true flag increments it. frame_idx is the global index into the image list (also 0-based), not reset within a traversal.

6. Example data & launching the server

An example stream sits under example_data/stream/28_metfloor_first150/ with 151 images and a pre-filled stream_annotations.json. A typical launching command from launch_stream_server.sh: 

source .venv/bin/activate

DATA_DIR=../metacam/data_v3/28_metfloor_first150
python stream/server.py $DATA_DIR/images ./label_28_metfloor.json \
    --output $DATA_DIR/stream_annotations.json --port 12346

Arguments:

  • $DATA_DIR/images — the folder of frames to annotate.
  • ./label_28_metfloor.json — the fixed label set for this stream.
  • --output — where to write/read stream_annotations.json. If it already exists, the server resumes from it.
  • --port — HTTP port to serve the GUI on.

Open http://<host>:<port>/ in a browser to start annotating.

7. Output format

One JSON file per stream, in stream order:

{
  "version": 2,
  "labels": ["tomato", "green pepper", "carrot", ...],
  "images": [
    {
      "file": "left_1768798238702970000.png",
      "new_traversal": false,
      "annotations": []
    },
    {
      "file": "left_1768798263201395000.png",
      "new_traversal": false,
      "annotations": [
        { "category": "green pepper",
          "point": { "x": 506.20, "y": 454.43 } }
      ]
    },
    {
      "file": "left_1769001234567890000.png",
      "new_traversal": true,
      "annotations": [ ... ]
    }
  ]
}
  • file is just the basename inside the image folder.
  • new_traversal is true only on the first frame of each new pass.
  • annotations[i].point is in image pixel coordinates (post-normalization to [0, 1] in newer versions — check version).
  • An entry with empty annotations means "I looked, nothing to label here".

To derive the per-object latest location, walk the images list, maintaining a running traversal_idx that increments at every new_traversal: true. For each labeled point, keep the most recent (frame_idx, traversal_idx) seen for that category.

8. Possible extensions

A single labeled point per object is a deliberately minimal signal — it is cheap to produce and enough for "where is the object now?" queries. The same protocol can be enriched along several axes if downstream tasks need more structure:

🧶Object semantic masks

Promote each click to a full segmentation mask (e.g. SAM-style click→mask).

Gives pixel extent and shape on top of position — SAM works mostly fine but human verification and mask refinement are expected.

📦3D recon + 3D bounding boxes

Reconstruct the scene to 3D pointcloud, and lift each 2D point into a 3D bounding box anchored in world coordinates.

Replaces (frame_idx, traversal_idx) with a metric 3D pose/coordinate, usefule for our metric methods.

🏷️Instance labels

Distinguish between individual instances of the same category (e.g. chair #1 vs chair #2), not just "chair".

Spatial understanding, change detection, or for tracking a specific object's trajectory across traversals.
